messages:
Ryan: FYI Aurora Health sent their security questionnaire and wants a simple network ask for the POC. They asked if we can do PrivateLink or VPC peering and what the firewall whitelist + pricing looks like. Any quick blockers?
Maya: Thanks — what's the POC topology? are they hitting our hosted API or spinning Redwood Private inside their VPC?
Ryan: Hosted API for now, but they want private connectivity for compliance. So we offered PrivateLink (interface endpoint) and also discussed VPC peering / transit options for a future private deploy. POC needs <500 qps, typical requests ~1–2k tokens.
Vishal: For hosted+PrivateLink: we provide an AWS interface endpoint on our side. Typical notes: PrivateLink hides our backend IPs (they connect to an ENI), so customer traffic terminates to our endpoint. Important: PrivateLink does NOT preserve the original source IP inside our infra — connections will appear from endpoint ENIs. If customer needs source-IP preservation for downstream ACLs, VPC peering (or dedicated Private deployment) is required.
Emily: Security note: their questionnaire also asks for egress IPs to allowlist and whether we use TLS mutual auth. We support TLS 1.2/1.3; mutual-tls is an enterprise addon for Private deployments only. For hosted PrivateLink we provide stable endpoint DNS and recommend allowlisting DNS + hosted endpoint EIPs if they cannot do DNS.
Carol: Quick pricing callout: PrivateLink has per-hour endpoint charges + per-GB data processing on AWS side. For us, we also apply a small connectivity surcharge for endpoint maintenance. VPC peering has no endpoint charge but can incur cross-AZ/data-transfer costs and requires more setup from both sides. For a short POC PrivateLink is usually faster to stand up.
Ryan: They also asked about firewall rules to pass to their netops — can we give a concise snippet?
Vishal: Sure — minimal outbound rules (they're allowing outbound from their clients to our endpoint):
```
# Allow outgoing to Redwood PrivateLink endpoint (TLS)
Allow: TCP 443 -> <redwood-privatelink-endpoint> (DNS CNAME)
Allow: ICMP type 3 for path MTU discovery (optional)
Allow: UDP 123 -> NTP (if they need time sync to external NTP)
```
If they insist on IPs, provide the endpoint EIP list we generate after provisioning.
Maya: Also call out SNI: they need to allow TLS SNI for the hostname we give (e.g., api.redwood-inference.com or privatelink.api.redwood-inference.internal). Some corp proxies do SNI allowlisting.
Emily: For the questionnaire Q: "Can you preserve client IP headers?" — answer: for PrivateLink/hosted: no. For VPC peering or Dedicated/Private deployments that run in customer VPC, yes (source IP preserved). Add a note about our audit logs capturing token-level request IDs for tracing.
Ryan: Good. They are also worried about egress IP stability for an allowlist. What do we normally give?
Carol: For PrivateLink endpoints we hand back a small set of EIPs per region (after we provision) that they can allowlist. For hosted public API it's many shared IPs so we recommend hostname allowlist or our published CDN ranges. For Dedicated or Private we can provide fixed EIPs as part of the contract.
Vishal: Operational blocker: if customer requires client IP preservation + minimal network change, that is contradictory — preserving IP typically requires routing their traffic directly into our VPC (peering/transit) or deploying Redwood in their account. Flag this as a sales constraint.
Maya: Action items for POC: (1) confirm whether Aurora can allowlist DNS + SNI vs only IPs, (2) confirm if they require src-IP preservation, (3) confirm expected egress bandwidth.
Ryan: I'll ping Aurora now asking those three. Also they asked about an example firewall JSON snippet for their CMDB. Can we provide a one-paragraph JSON example?
Carol: Quick example (they can edit values):
```json
{
  "name": "allow-redwood-privatelink",
  "direction": "egress",
  "protocol": "TCP",
  "ports": "443",
  "destination": "privatelink-eu-west-1.api.redwood-inference.internal",
  "notes": "Allow TLS to Redwood PrivateLink endpoint. If IP allowlisting required, replace destination with provided EIPs."
}
```
Maya: Security runbook note: we also suggest enabling short-lived API keys for the POC and adding request-level logging enabled in the console so their infosec team can validate.
Emily: I can answer the questionnaire items about encryption in transit, key management, and audit logs. Send the doc and I'll fill the sections that reference network assumptions.
Ryan: Thanks all — I'll: ping Aurora for the three confirmations, attach the firewall JSON example, and ask netops if they can accept DNS/SNI allowlist. Will update thread. :thumbsup:
infra-bot: Created ticket RED-5682 to provision a sandbox PrivateLink endpoint in us-east-1 for Aurora POC. ETA 2 business days.
Ryan: Noted infra ticket. ETA fine for their timeline. I'll update Aurora and loop in their netops on the ticket.
Maya: Awesome — if they push for preserving src IP during the POC escalate to me; we'll propose a short-term Dedicated eval or peering with NAT64 depending on their environment.
Ryan: Will do. Closing loop after their reply.
